claims.text: The Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline is an equiatomic FCC alloy produced by thermomechanical processing.
The equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets can be produced as single-phase FCC materials using processing identical to the quinary baseline.
Removing one or two elements from the quinary alloy changes local lattice distortion and short-range chemical order.
Differences in local lattice distortion and short-range chemical order primarily explain differences in deformation and failure among these alloys.
Local lattice distortion and short-range chemical order modify barriers to dislocation motion and alter active slip mechanisms.
The quinary alloy has more heterogeneous internal stress fields than its reduced-constituent subsets.
The quinary alloy has more pronounced short-range chemical ordering than its quaternary and ternary subsets.
The proposed internal stress fields and short-range ordering impede dislocation glide in the quinary alloy.
Impeded dislocation glide gives the quinary alloy higher strain hardening.
Reduced-constituent alloys have less lattice distortion and less short-range ordering than the quinary alloy.
Quaternary and ternary alloys will have lower yield strength than the quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary alloys will exhibit modified strain-hardening profiles relative to the quinary baseline.
The yield strengths of quaternary and ternary alloys may be 10–20% lower than that of the quinary alloy.
The comparison is intended to apply to alloys with comparable single-phase FCC structures, identical thermomechanical processing, room-temperature testing, and similar deformation rates.

A lack of systematic mechanical-property differences correlated with measured lattice distortion and short-range order, or statistically indistinguishable deformation responses across the systems, would falsify the hypothesis.
